p: Good evening, my dear friend, and welcome to the foothills. Base camp is behind us and the path now rises gently. Tonight we meet the central idea of algebra: using a letter to stand for a number. It sounds abstract. It is not. You have done it all your life.
## A number with a hidden face

Suppose I say: I am thinking of a number. I add three and get ten. What is my number? You know at once: seven. You have just done algebra. In the language of algebra, we give the unknown number a name, usually the letter x, and write what we know.
In plain words: some number, plus three, makes ten. The letter is simply a box with a question mark on it, waiting to be opened. Solving the equation means finding what is in the box. Seven.
?? While I pour. I think of a number and double it, and get eighteen. What is it?
=> Nine. Written as algebra: two x equals eighteen.
## The balance scale

An equation is like an old-fashioned balance scale, the sort with two pans that every grocer used in my day. The equals sign is the pivot in the middle. Whatever is on the left weighs the same as whatever is on the right.

The great rule of the balance: whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other, or the scale tips. Take three ounces off the left pan, and you must take three off the right. That rule is the whole secret of solving equations, and we shall use it constantly.

Picture x plus three equals ten on the scale: a mystery parcel and three one-ounce weights on the left, ten one-ounce weights on the right. Take three weights off each side. Now the parcel alone balances seven weights. The parcel weighs seven.
## The equals sign

That sign has a lovely history. It was invented by a Welshman, Robert Recorde, in a book of 1557 called The Whetstone of Witte. He was tired of writing "is equal to" again and again, so he drew two parallel lines, because, as he put it in the spelling of his day, no two things can be more equal. Two parallel lines, forever side by side, never meeting, perfectly equal. I think it is the most charming reason ever given for a symbol.
## Al-Khwarizmi and al-jabr

Algebra as a subject takes its name from a book written in Baghdad around the year 820 by Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, whom we met in the story of zero. His book had a title meaning something like The Compendious Book on Calculation by Restoring and Balancing. The Arabic for restoring is al-jabr. It meant moving a subtracted quantity to the other side of an equation, where it becomes added, restoring it. That one word became algebra.

Curiously, al-Khwarizmi used no letters at all. He wrote everything in words: "a square and ten roots are equal to thirty-nine units". The use of letters came much later. François Viète in France, in the late sixteenth century, used letters systematically, and René Descartes, in 1637, made it the custom to use x, y and z for unknowns, from the end of the alphabet, and a, b, c for known quantities, from the beginning.
## Letters as any number

A letter can also stand for any number at all, not one particular unknown. When we say that a plus b equals b plus a, we mean it is true whatever numbers a and b are. That is a law, a pattern that always holds. Algebra lets us state such patterns once, for all numbers, instead of checking them one by one forever.
?? Is it true that x plus x equals two x, whatever number x is?
=> Yes. Any number added to itself is two of that number.
## Writing algebra

A few habits of algebraic writing. We leave out the times sign between a number and a letter: three x means three times x. We write the number first: three x, not x three. And x times x is written x squared.
In plain words: three times some number, plus two. If x is four, this is twelve plus two, fourteen. If x is ten, thirty-two.
## A Mrs Blewitt puzzle

Mrs Blewitt bought three loaves and a pot of jam costing one pound, and paid four pounds altogether. What did a loaf cost? Call the price of a loaf x. Three x plus one equals four. Take one pound off each side: three x equals three. Divide both sides by three: x equals one. A pound a loaf. She considers this robbery, but the algebra is sound.
?? Five pens and a two-pound notebook cost seven pounds. What did one pen cost?
=> Five x plus two equals seven. Take two from each side: five x equals five. So x equals one. A pound a pen.
## Summary

A letter stands for an unknown number, or for any number. An equation is a balance scale, and whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. The equals sign was invented by Robert Recorde in 1557, and algebra is named after al-jabr in al-Khwarizmi's book. Next time, the grammar of algebra: terms, expressions and gathering like with like. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we become locksmiths. An equation is a locked box with the unknown number inside, and solving it means picking the lock, one tumbler at a time. The tool for every tumbler is the balance scale: whatever we do to one side, we do to the other.
## One step
Something plus five makes twelve. To get x alone, undo the plus five by taking five from both sides. x equals seven.
Four times something is twenty. Undo the multiplying by dividing both sides by four. x equals five.
Every operation has its undoing partner. Adding is undone by subtracting; multiplying by dividing; and so on.
?? While I pour. Solve x minus three equals nine.
=> Add three to both sides. x equals twelve.
## Two steps

Here x has been through two operations: first multiplied by three, then four taken away. To undo them, work backwards, like taking off your boots before your socks: first undo the last thing done. Add four to both sides.
Then divide both sides by three.
Check by substitution: three fives are fifteen, minus four is eleven. The balance holds.
A good image: x has put on a waistcoat and then a coat. To get back to x, take off the coat first, then the waistcoat. The last thing on is the first thing off.
?? Solve two x plus seven equals nineteen.
=> Take seven from both sides: two x equals twelve. Divide by two: x equals six.
## Letters on both sides
Now there are x's on both pans of the scale. Gather them on one side by taking three x from both sides.
Now it is a two-step equation. Take two from both sides: two x equals eight. Divide by two: x equals four. Check: five fours plus two is twenty-two; three fours plus ten is twenty-two. Balanced.
?? Solve seven x minus three equals four x plus nine.
=> Take four x from both sides: three x minus three equals nine. Add three: three x equals twelve. Divide: x equals four.
## Brackets in equations

Two ways. Expand first: two x plus six equals sixteen, so two x equals ten, so x equals five. Or, more elegantly, divide both sides by two straight away: x plus three equals eight, so x equals five. Both are right; choose whichever path looks smoother.
## Fractions in equations
Something divided by four is three. Undo the dividing by multiplying both sides by four. x equals twelve.

Multiply both sides by three: x plus two equals fifteen. Then take two: x equals thirteen. Notice that the three divided the whole of x plus two, the whole parcel above the line, so we multiply first to release the parcel.
?? Solve x over five, minus one, equals three.
=> Add one to both sides: x over five equals four. Multiply by five: x equals twenty.
## Word problems

A tradesman's puzzle. A carpenter cuts a plank twenty feet long into two pieces, one of them four feet longer than the other. How long is each? Let the shorter piece be x. The longer is x plus four. Together they make twenty.
So two x plus four equals twenty, two x equals sixteen, x equals eight. The pieces are eight feet and twelve feet. Check: twelve is four more than eight, and together they make twenty.
The skill in word problems is translating English into algebra: name the unknown, write each fact as an expression, and set up the balance. After that, the locksmith's tools do the rest.
?? Mrs Blewitt is three times as old as her nephew, and together their ages make sixty-four. How old is the nephew?
=> Let the nephew be x. Mrs Blewitt is three x. So four x equals sixty-four, and x equals sixteen. The nephew is sixteen, and Mrs Blewitt forty-eight, which she would prefer I had not mentioned.
## Summary

Solve by doing the same to both sides until the letter stands alone. Undo operations in reverse order: coat before waistcoat. Gather letters on one side first. Clear brackets and fractions by expanding or multiplying. Always check by substitution. Next time, the laws of indices, the rules for handling powers. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. So far our equations have been linear: x appears only to the first power, and the graph is a straight line. Tonight the squares come in. Quadratic equations, named from the Latin quadratus, a square, are where algebra gets its first real teeth, and they have been solved, in one way or another, for nearly four thousand years.
## What a quadratic is
A quadratic expression has an x squared term, and no higher power.

In plain words: some number of x squared, plus some number of x, plus a plain number. The letters a, b and c stand for fixed numbers, called coefficients, and a must not be nought, or the square would vanish.
Here a is one, b is minus five, and c is six.
?? While I pour. In two x squared plus seven x minus four, what are a, b and c?
=> a is two, b is seven, and c is minus four.
## Where quadratics come from

Quadratics arise whenever areas are involved, because area multiplies two lengths. A field is three yards longer than it is wide, and its area is forty square yards. How wide is it? If the width is x, the length is x plus three, and
which expands to x squared plus three x equals forty. A quadratic. The answer is five: five times eight is forty.
They also arise in motion. A stone dropped from a height falls a distance proportional to the square of the time, as Galileo found. Ask when it hits the ground, and you have a quadratic.
## Two answers
A linear equation has one answer. A quadratic may have two. Consider:
x could be three, or minus three, since minus three squared is also nine. Two answers. Mathematicians call the answers roots or solutions.

Some quadratics have only one: x squared equals nought has only nought. And some have none among the ordinary numbers: x squared equals minus one, since no ordinary number squared is negative. Aunt Hester, I might add, would have been gratified to hear that there is something negative numbers cannot do.
?? What are the solutions of x squared equals twenty-five?
=> Five and minus five.
## The Babylonians

Clay tablets from Babylon, nearly four thousand years old, contain problems like this: I have added the area and the side of my square, and it is three quarters. What is the side? In our symbols, x squared plus x equals three quarters. The scribes gave a recipe, step by step, which amounts to the method we still teach, and the answer is a half. They had no algebra symbols and no negative numbers, but they had the method.
## Al-Khwarizmi's square
In Baghdad around 820, al-Khwarizmi, whose book on al-jabr gave algebra its name, solved quadratics by geometry. His famous example: a square and ten roots equal thirty-nine.

Picture it, as he did. A square with side x. Now take the ten x and split it into four strips, each x long and two and a half wide, and attach one to each side of the square. The shape is now a cross, with area thirty-nine. Its four corners are missing: four little squares, each two and a half by two and a half, six and a quarter each, twenty-five altogether. Fill them in. Now you have a complete large square, with area thirty-nine plus twenty-five, sixty-four. Its side is eight. And that side is x plus two and a half plus two and a half, which is x plus five. So x plus five is eight, and x is three.

He literally completed the square. We still use that phrase, and in two lectures' time I shall show you the algebra version. For now, admire the picture: the geometry of a carpenter, solving an equation.
?? Check al-Khwarizmi's answer. Is three squared plus ten threes equal to thirty-nine?
=> Nine plus thirty is thirty-nine. Splendid.
He found only the positive answer, three. There is another, minus thirteen, which he would not have counted; negative answers were not respectable for many centuries.
## Three methods ahead

There are three standard ways to solve a quadratic, and the next lectures take them in turn. Factorising, using the brown-paper parcels of the primer, which is quick when it works. Completing the square, al-Khwarizmi's way, which always works. And the quadratic formula, which is completing the square done once and for all, so you never need to do it again.
## Summary

A quadratic has an x squared as its highest power: a x squared plus b x plus c. Quadratic equations come from areas and motion, and may have two, one or no ordinary solutions. The Babylonians solved them four thousand years ago, and al-Khwarizmi solved them by completing a square of tiles. Next time, solving quadratics by factorising. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Every language has a grammar, and algebra is a language. Tonight we learn its parts of speech: terms, expressions and equations, and the most useful habit in all algebra, gathering like with like.
## Terms and expressions

A term is a single piece: a number, a letter, or numbers and letters multiplied together. Three x is a term. Five is a term. Seven x squared is a term. Terms are joined into an expression by plus and minus signs.

In plain words: three x, plus two y, minus five. Three terms. The number in front of a letter is called its coefficient: three is the coefficient of x. A term with no letter at all, like minus five, is called a constant, because it never changes, whatever x and y may be.
An expression is like a phrase. An equation is like a sentence: it has an equals sign and makes a claim that two expressions are equal.
?? While I pour. In the expression five x minus four y plus one, what is the coefficient of y?
=> Minus four. The sign belongs to the term.
## Like with like
Here is the habit. Terms with exactly the same letters, raised to the same powers, are called like terms, and they can be combined by adding or subtracting their coefficients.
In plain words: three of something and five of the same something make eight of it. Three apples and five apples are eight apples.

But x and y are different things. Three x plus two y cannot be simplified, any more than three apples and two oranges can be called five apploranges. Mrs Blewitt, who keeps her accounts in separate columns for the butcher, the baker and the coal merchant, would recognise the principle at once.
Gather the x terms: four x and two x are six x. Gather the y terms: three y minus one y is two y. Notice that y on its own means one y.
?? Simplify seven a plus two b minus three a plus five b.
=> The a terms: seven a minus three a is four a. The b terms: two b plus five b is seven b. Four a plus seven b.
## Powers make terms different
Here is a subtle point. x and x squared are not like terms. x might be the length of a fence, and x squared the area of a field. You cannot add a length to an area and get a single number of either.
Two x squared and one x squared make three x squared. The three x stands apart, unmoved.
## Multiplying terms
Multiplying is different from adding. When you multiply terms, multiply the numbers and put the letters together.
⟦3x\times 4y=12xy⟧
Three times four is twelve, and x times y is written x y. And x times x is x squared.
⟦2x\times 5x=10x^{2}⟧
?? Simplify three a times two a.
=> Three times two is six, and a times a is a squared. Six a squared.
## Order of letters

By custom, letters in a term are written in alphabetical order: x y, not y x. Since multiplying does not care about order, they are the same thing, but alphabetical order makes it easier to spot like terms. Three x y and two y x are like terms, making five x y.
## Expressions as instructions

Here is a helpful way to think. An expression is a set of instructions, a recipe. Three x plus two says: take a number, multiply by three, add two. The recipe does not tell you the answer until you know what x is. Simplifying an expression means rewriting the recipe in fewer steps, without changing what it produces. Four x plus three plus two x minus one gives exactly the same result as six x plus two, for every possible x. But the second recipe is shorter, and Mrs Blewitt approves of short recipes.
?? Write a simplified recipe for: x plus x plus x plus four plus one.
=> Three x plus five.
## Summary

Terms are joined by plus and minus into expressions; an equation says two expressions are equal. Like terms have the same letters and powers and can be combined by adding coefficients. Unlike terms, such as x and y, or x and x squared, stay apart. When multiplying terms, multiply the numbers and gather the letters. Next time, substitution: putting numbers into the recipe to see what comes out. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Last time I described an expression as a recipe. Tonight we cook. Substitution means putting particular numbers in place of the letters, and working out what the expression is worth. It is how formulas are used in the real world, by engineers, actuaries, navigators and, on at least one occasion, by Mrs Blewitt, calculating how much coal to order for the winter.
## The basic idea
If x is four, what is three x plus two? Replace x with four.
In plain words: three fours are twelve, plus two is fourteen. That is substitution. The letter steps aside and the number takes its seat.
?? While I pour. If y is five, what is four y minus seven?
=> Four times five is twenty, minus seven is thirteen.
## Two letters
With more than one letter, substitute each.
If a is five and b is two, this is two fives plus three twos: ten plus six, sixteen.
## Mind the royal kitchen
The order of operations matters greatly here. If x is three, what is two x squared?

The head chef, the power, goes first: three squared is nine. Then the cooks: two times nine is eighteen. Not six squared, which would be thirty-six. The square applies only to the x, not to the two. If we wanted the two included, we would have written bracket two x, squared.
?? If x is four, what is x squared plus three x?
=> Sixteen plus twelve, which is twenty-eight.
## Negative numbers in brackets
Substituting a negative number needs care, and here our brackets earn their keep. If x is minus three, what is x squared?
Put the minus three in a protective bracket before squaring. Minus three times minus three is plus nine. Without the bracket, you might write minus three squared and get minus nine, which is wrong.
?? If x is minus two, what is five minus x?
=> Five minus, bracket, minus two. Taking away a negative means adding: five plus two, seven.
## Real formulas
Formulas in science and daily life are substitution waiting to happen. The area of a rectangle is length times width.
⟦A=lw⟧
A room twelve feet long and ten feet wide has an area of a hundred and twenty square feet.
To turn a temperature in degrees Celsius into degrees Fahrenheit, multiply by nine fifths and add thirty-two.

If it is twenty degrees Celsius: nine fifths of twenty is thirty-six, plus thirty-two is sixty-eight degrees Fahrenheit. A pleasant English summer's day. In my time the Fahrenheit scale was what everyone in Britain used, and Celsius, then usually called centigrade, was for scientists and the French.
?? What is a hundred degrees Celsius in Fahrenheit?
=> Nine fifths of a hundred is a hundred and eighty, plus thirty-two is two hundred and twelve. The boiling point of water.
## A formula for the cab fare
Imagine a hansom cab that charges a shilling to start and sixpence a mile. In your decimal money, let us say a pound to start and fifty pence a mile. The fare for m miles is:

A journey of six miles costs one plus three, four pounds. The formula is a small machine: put in miles, out comes cost. We shall see in the lectures on functions that this is exactly what a function is.
## Checking an answer

Substitution has another great use: checking. If you have solved an equation and think x is seven, put seven back into the equation and see whether both sides balance. If they do, your answer is right. Teachers forget to tell people this, and it is the most useful habit an algebraist can have.
?? Someone claims that x equals four solves three x minus five equals seven. Check by substitution.
=> Three times four is twelve, minus five is seven. Both sides are seven. The claim is correct.
## Summary

Substitution replaces letters with numbers. Follow the order of operations, with powers before multiplying. Put negative numbers in brackets to keep their signs. Formulas everywhere are substitution in waiting. And substitution is the way to check any solution. Next time we solve equations properly, with the balance scale. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight a lecture of laws, but kindly ones. Powers, which we met at base camp, obey a few simple rules called the laws of indices. They are not arbitrary decrees; each follows directly from what a power means, and I shall show you why, so that you never need to memorise them blindly.
## The first law: multiplying
What is x cubed times x squared? x cubed is three x's multiplied together. x squared is two more. Altogether, five x's multiplied.
So when multiplying powers of the same base, add the indices. Three plus two is five.
⟦a^{m}\times a^{n}=a^{m+n}⟧
In plain words: a to the m, times a to the n, is a to the m plus n. We used this already in standard form, when ten cubed times ten to the five made ten to the eight.
?? While I pour. What is two to the power of four times two to the power of three? Give it as a power, and as a number.
=> Two to the power of seven, which is a hundred and twenty-eight.
A warning: the bases must be the same. x squared times y cubed cannot be combined this way. Different bases, different families.
## The second law: dividing
What is x to the five divided by x squared? Write it as a fraction: five x's on top, two underneath. Two x's on top cancel with the two underneath, leaving three.
So when dividing, subtract the indices. Five take two is three.
?? What is y to the power of nine divided by y to the power of four?
=> y to the power of five. Nine take four.
## The third law: a power of a power
What is x squared, all cubed? That is x squared times x squared times x squared: two plus two plus two, six.
So a power of a power multiplies the indices. Two times three is six.
## The power of nought

Now something surprising. What is x squared divided by x squared? Anything divided by itself is one. But by the second law, it is x to the power of two take two, x to the nought. So x to the power of nought must be one.

Any number, except nought itself, raised to the power of nought, is one. People find this odd at first. Think of it as: multiplying no x's at all leaves you with one, the starting point of multiplication, just as adding nothing leaves you at nought. Ten to the power of nought is one. A million to the power of nought is one. Euclid the cat to the power of nought is, I suppose, one cat, which is about as much cat as anyone needs.
## Negative powers

What is x squared divided by x to the five? By the second law, x to the power of two take five, x to the minus three. But as a fraction, two x's on top cancel with two of the five underneath, leaving one over x cubed.
So a negative power means one over the positive power. We saw this with standard form, where ten to the minus three meant one thousandth.
?? What is two to the power of minus two?
=> One over two squared, which is one quarter.
## Fractional powers, briefly

One more, for the curious, which you may skip without guilt. What could x to the power of a half mean? By the first law, x to the half times x to the half is x to the one, which is x. So x to the half, multiplied by itself, gives x. That is exactly what a square root does.

So a power of a half is a square root. Nine to the power of a half is three. A power of a third is a cube root. These fractional powers were made popular by Isaac Newton, who used them freely in the 1660s and 1670s, and they will be useful in calculus.
## Numbers in front
When terms have numbers in front, deal with the numbers and the letters separately.
Three times four is twelve; x squared times x to the five is x to the seven.
?? Simplify ten x to the six divided by two x squared.
=> Ten divided by two is five; x to the six divided by x squared is x to the four. Five x to the four.
## Summary

Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices. Dividing subtracts them. A power of a power multiplies them. Anything to the power of nought is one, and a negative power means one over. A power of a half is a square root. Each law follows from what a power means, so you can always rebuild it from scratch. Next time, rearranging formulas: making any letter the subject. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we learn to turn formulas inside out. A formula usually tells you how to find one thing from others: the area from the length and width, the fare from the miles. But sometimes you know the area and want the width. Rearranging a formula, or changing its subject, lets the same formula answer a different question.
## The subject of a formula
The subject is the letter standing alone, usually on the left.
⟦A=lw⟧
Here A, the area, is the subject. If we know the area is a hundred and twenty square feet and the length is twelve, what is the width? Divide both sides by l.
⟦w=\frac{A}{l}⟧
Now w is the subject. A hundred and twenty divided by twelve is ten feet.
Rearranging is exactly like solving an equation, except that the other letters stay as letters. We use the same balance-scale rule: do the same to both sides.
?? While I pour. Make l the subject of A equals l w.
=> Divide both sides by w: l equals A over w.
## Two steps
The cab fare formula from our lecture on substitution:

Suppose a fare came to four pounds. How many miles? Rearrange to make m the subject. Take one from both sides: C minus one equals nought point five m. Divide both sides by nought point five, which is the same as doubling.
Four pounds gives two times three, six miles.
## Reversing Fahrenheit
The temperature formula:

To get Celsius from Fahrenheit, undo in reverse order. The last thing done was adding thirty-two, so take thirty-two from both sides. Then the C was multiplied by nine fifths, so multiply both sides by five ninths.

In plain words: take away thirty-two, then multiply by five ninths. Sixty-eight degrees Fahrenheit: sixty-eight take thirty-two is thirty-six, and five ninths of thirty-six is twenty. Twenty degrees Celsius. Notice the brackets: the five ninths must multiply the whole of F minus thirty-two, the whole parcel.
?? Use it. What is fifty degrees Fahrenheit in Celsius?
=> Fifty take thirty-two is eighteen, and five ninths of eighteen is ten. Ten degrees Celsius.
## Squares and roots
The area of a circle:
To find the radius from the area, divide both sides by pi, then take the square root of both sides, since the square root undoes squaring.
⟦r=\sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}⟧
The roof of the square root covers the whole fraction.
Another example, from mechanics: kinetic energy is half the mass times the speed squared.
To find the speed: double both sides, divide by m, then take the square root.
⟦v=\sqrt{\frac{2E}{m}}⟧
?? Make x the subject of y equals x squared minus five.
=> Add five to both sides: y plus five equals x squared. Take the square root: x equals the square root of y plus five.
## When the subject appears twice

Occasionally the letter you want appears in two places. Then gather the terms containing it together, and take it out as a common factor, a parcel. That uses the factorising from part seven of the primer. I mention it only so you know it can be done; we shall meet it when it is needed.
## Why this matters

Rearranging formulas is daily bread for engineers and scientists. A Victorian engineer like Isambard Kingdom Brunel, designing the Clifton Suspension Bridge near my old home in Bristol, used formulas relating loads, lengths and stresses, turning them about to find whichever quantity was unknown. The bridge, I may say, was designed by Brunel but completed only in 1864, after his death, by other engineers as a memorial to him. Every time I crossed it, I gave silent thanks for algebra done correctly.
## Summary

The subject of a formula is the letter standing alone. To change the subject, use the balance rule, undoing the operations around the new subject in reverse order. Square roots undo squares. Brackets keep parcels together when multiplying or dividing whole sides. Next comes a refresher for those who want the whole first stretch of algebra in one sitting, and then the story of Charles Babbage and Ada Lovelace. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight a detective story. There are two culprits, two unknown numbers, and a single clue will never catch both. But two good clues, taken together, will. Equations that must be true at the same time are called simultaneous equations, and solving them is one of the most satisfying pieces of work in the foothills.
## Why one clue is not enough
Mrs Blewitt bought apples and pears, ten pieces of fruit altogether. How many of each? With only that clue, it could be five and five, or seven and three, or nought and ten. Many answers.
Now a second clue: she bought four more apples than pears.
Now there is only one answer. Seven apples and three pears. Check: seven plus three is ten, seven minus three is four. Both clues satisfied at once, simultaneously.
## Elimination

How did I find it without guessing? Look at the two equations together. One has plus y, the other minus y. If I add the two equations, left side to left side and right side to right side, the y's cancel out, eliminated.
So x is seven. Then, from the first clue, seven plus y is ten, so y is three.
Adding equations is allowed because both are balances. If two scales are each level, putting the contents of both left pans together and both right pans together still balances.
?? While I pour. Solve a plus b equals twelve, and a minus b equals two.
=> Add: two a equals fourteen, so a is seven. Then b is five.
## Making the numbers match
Often the letters do not cancel so neatly.

Both have two x. Subtract the second from the first: the two x's vanish, three y minus y is two y, and thirteen minus seven is six. So two y equals six, and y is three. Then two x plus three is seven, so two x is four, and x is two.

Sometimes neither letter matches. Then multiply a whole equation by a number to make them match. If one equation has x and the other three x, multiply the first by three, every term, both sides, and then subtract. It is like converting shillings to pence before adding: get everything in the same units first.
?? Solve three x plus y equals eleven, and x plus y equals five.
=> Subtract the second from the first: two x equals six, so x is three. Then y is two.
## Substitution
The second method uses what we learned about substitution. Take one equation and rearrange it so one letter stands alone.
The first already tells us what y is. Put two x minus one in place of y in the second, in a protective bracket.
So five x minus one is fourteen, five x is fifteen, x is three. Then y is two times three minus one, five.
Substitution is best when one letter is already alone or nearly so. Elimination is best when the letters line up in columns. Both arrive at the same answer, as two good detectives should.
## A word problem
At a Mechanics' Institute tea, cups of tea cost three pence and buns five pence. A party of workers bought eight items and paid thirty-two pence. How many buns?
Let t be teas and b be buns. Eight items:
Thirty-two pence:

Multiply the first by three: three t plus three b equals twenty-four. Subtract from the second: two b equals eight, so b is four. Four buns and four teas. Check: twelve pence plus twenty pence is thirty-two. I remember such teas fondly; the buns were always gone before the tea.
## Pictures in the mind

Each equation in two letters describes a straight line, as we shall hear in the lectures on graphs. The solution of two simultaneous equations is the point where the two lines cross. Two lines generally cross at exactly one point, which is why two clues give one answer. If the lines are parallel they never cross, and the clues contradict each other: there is no solution. If the two equations are secretly the same line, there are endless solutions, because the second clue told us nothing new.
## Summary

Two unknowns need two independent clues. Elimination adds or subtracts equations to remove a letter, after multiplying to make coefficients match if needed. Substitution rearranges one equation and puts it into the other. Always check in both equations. And the answer is where two lines cross. Next time, logic words: and, or, not, if and then. Good evening, my dear friend. So far our balance scale has always been level. Tonight we let it tip. An inequality says that one side is heavier, larger, than the other. It sounds like a small change, and mostly it is, with one famous exception that catches out nearly everyone once.
## The four signs
x is less than five. The sign is like an arrowhead, or a crocodile's mouth if you were taught that way: the open end faces the larger side. The pointed end points at the smaller.
x is greater than five.
⟦x\le 5⟧
x is less than or equal to five. The little line under the sign is half an equals sign. Similarly, greater than or equal to.

These signs came into use in a book by Thomas Harriot, published in 1631, ten years after his death. Harriot was an Englishman who also sailed to Virginia in the 1580s; his symbols were slightly different from ours, but the idea stuck.
?? While I pour. Is minus seven less than minus two?
=> Yes. On the number line minus seven is further left. Aunt Hester would have been horrified to hear that minus seven is smaller, despite looking bigger, but it is.
## Solutions are ranges

The equation x plus three equals eight has one answer, five. The inequality x plus three is less than eight has many: every number less than five. Four, nought, minus a hundred, four point nine nine. The answer is a range.
Solve it just like an equation: take three from both sides.
In the interval brackets from part eight of the primer, that is the interval from minus infinity to five, both ends round, because five itself is not included.
## Most moves are safe

Adding or subtracting the same thing on both sides keeps an inequality true. If I am shorter than you, and we both stand on the same box, I am still shorter. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive number is also safe: if I have fewer shillings than you, and our money is doubled, I still have fewer.
Add two: three x is greater than or equal to twelve. Divide by three: x is greater than or equal to four.
?? Solve two x plus one is less than nine.
=> Take one: two x is less than eight. Divide by two: x is less than four.
## The famous exception
Here it is. Two is less than five. Multiply both sides by minus one. Minus two and minus five. Which is smaller now? Minus five. So minus two is greater than minus five. The order has flipped.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the order, so you must reverse the sign. A mirror at nought swaps left and right on the number line.
Divide both sides by minus two, and flip the sign.
Check with a number: try minus four, which is less than minus three. Minus two times minus four is plus eight, and eight is greater than six. Correct.
?? Solve minus x is less than or equal to four.
=> Multiply by minus one and flip: x is greater than or equal to minus four.

If you prefer to avoid the exception altogether, there is a trick: move the letter term to the side where it will be positive. Minus two x greater than six: add two x to both sides and take six from both sides. Minus six is greater than two x, so minus three is greater than x. Same answer, no flipping required.
## Double inequalities
Sometimes x is trapped between two numbers.
x is greater than minus one and less than or equal to four. In interval brackets: round at minus one, square at four. You solve these by doing the same thing to all three parts.
Take one from all three parts: two is less than two x, which is less than ten. Divide all by two: one is less than x, which is less than five.
## Whole number solutions

Sometimes we want only whole numbers. If x is a whole number and minus one is less than x, which is less than or equal to three, the possibilities are nought, one, two and three. A set, which we would write in curly braces.
## Summary

Inequality signs point to the smaller side. Solve inequalities like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative, or move terms to avoid it. Solutions are ranges, written with interval brackets or, for whole numbers, as sets. Next time, simultaneous equations: two unknowns at once. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight the quickest method for solving quadratics, when it works, and it relies on the brown-paper parcels of the primer, and on one little fact about nought that is almost too obvious to say.
## The nought trick
If two numbers multiply to give nought, then at least one of them must be nought. There is no other way to get nought by multiplying. Three times something is nought only if that something is nought.
means A is nought or B is nought, or both. This simple fact is the key to the whole method.
## Brackets that make nought

Two parcels multiplied together give nought. So one of the parcels must be nought. Either x minus two is nought, giving x equals two, or x minus three is nought, giving x equals three. Two solutions, found in a moment.
?? While I pour. Solve, bracket x plus four, times bracket x minus one, equals nought.
=> x plus four is nought gives x equals minus four, and x minus one is nought gives x equals one.
## Getting into brackets
So the trick is to get a quadratic into a product of brackets. That is factorising, part seven of the primer. Recall that when we expand:

In plain words: the two numbers in the brackets add up to the middle coefficient and multiply to the last number. So to factorise x squared plus b x plus c, we hunt for two numbers that multiply to give c and add to give b.
## An example

We want two numbers that multiply to six and add to minus five. Pairs that multiply to six: one and six, two and three, and their negatives. Minus two and minus three multiply to plus six and add to minus five. Found them.
So x is two or three. Check: four minus ten plus six is nought. Nine minus fifteen plus six is nought. Both splendid.
?? Factorise x squared plus seven x plus ten, and solve it equal to nought.
=> Two and five multiply to ten and add to seven. Bracket x plus two, bracket x plus five. Solutions minus two and minus five.
## Signs: a little guide

If the last number is positive, both numbers have the same sign, the sign of the middle coefficient. If the last number is negative, the numbers have opposite signs, and the larger one carries the sign of the middle coefficient.
Multiply to minus twelve, add to plus one: four and minus three. So bracket x plus four, bracket x minus three, and x is minus four or three.
## Get nought on one side first
The nought trick only works if one side is nought. If the field problem gives x squared plus three x equals forty, first take forty from both sides.

Multiply to minus forty, add to three: eight and minus five. So x is minus eight or five. The field cannot have a negative width, so the answer is five yards. Real problems sometimes throw away one root; that is common sense, not mathematics.
## Special cases
If there is no plain number, take out x as a common factor.

x times, bracket x minus seven, equals nought. So x is nought or seven. Never divide both sides by x here; you would lose the solution nought, and nought is a perfectly respectable answer, whatever Aunt Hester thought of it.
And the difference of two squares, from the primer:
So x squared minus nine equals nought gives three and minus three.
?? Solve x squared minus forty-nine equals nought.
=> Bracket x minus seven, bracket x plus seven. x is seven or minus seven.
## When the x squared has a number

If the quadratic starts with two x squared or more, factorising is a little more fiddly, and it is often quicker to use the formula I shall give you next time. Do not be discouraged if a quadratic will not factorise neatly; most, in real life, do not. The method is a lovely shortcut for the tidy cases, not a test of character.
## Summary

If a product is nought, a factor is nought. So get nought on one side, factorise into brackets, and set each bracket to nought. To factorise x squared plus b x plus c, find two numbers multiplying to c and adding to b. Take out x when there is no plain number, and use the difference of two squares when you can. Next time, completing the square and the famous formula. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight, the most famous formula in school algebra, and, I hope, the end of any fear of it. We shall not simply recite it. We shall build it, from al-Khwarizmi's tiles, so that you understand every piece. Then you may recite it with a clear conscience.
## Completing the square, in algebra
Remember al-Khwarizmi's picture: a square and ten roots, to which he added four corner tiles to make a perfect square. Here is the same idea in symbols. Notice that:
So x squared plus ten x is just, bracket x plus five, squared, minus twenty-five. The five is half of ten. In general:
⟦x^{2}+bx=\left(x+\frac{b}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{b^{2}}{4}⟧

In plain words: x squared plus b x equals, x plus half b, all squared, minus the square of half b. Halve the middle coefficient, put it in the bracket with x, square the bracket, and take away the extra corner you added.
## Solving with it

Complete the square: bracket x plus five, squared, minus twenty-five, equals thirty-nine. Add twenty-five: bracket x plus five, squared, equals sixty-four. Take the square root of both sides, remembering both signs: x plus five is eight or minus eight. So x is three, or minus thirteen. Al-Khwarizmi's answer, and the one he did not count.
?? While I pour. Complete the square for x squared plus six x. What do you put in the bracket, and what do you take away?
=> Half of six is three. Bracket x plus three, squared, minus nine.
## The formula

Now do it once and for all, with letters instead of numbers. Start with a x squared plus b x plus c equals nought, divide by a, complete the square, take the square root, and tidy up. I shall spare you the tidying, which is just careful algebra of the kind you already know, and give you the result.
$$ x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}
In plain words: x equals minus b, plus or minus the square root of b squared minus four a c, all over two a. The plus or minus gives the two solutions: one with plus, one with minus.
Some schoolchildren sing it to a tune. I have heard Pop Goes the Weasel used, and I will not attempt it here, for Euclid the cat has very sensitive ears.
## Using the formula

a is one, b is minus five, c is six. Minus b is five. b squared is twenty-five; four a c is twenty-four; twenty-five minus twenty-four is one, and its square root is one. Two a is two. So x is five plus one over two, which is three, or five minus one over two, which is two. The same answers factorising gave us.
?? Use the formula for x squared plus four x minus five equals nought. First, what is b squared minus four a c?
=> Sixteen minus four times one times minus five: sixteen plus twenty, thirty-six. Its square root is six. So x is minus four plus six over two, one, or minus four minus six over two, minus five.
## An ugly one
The formula shines when factorising fails.

b squared minus four a c is four plus four, eight. The square root of eight is about two point eight three. So x is two plus two point eight three over two, about two point four one, or two minus two point eight three over two, about minus nought point four one. No neat brackets would ever have found those. In exact form, x is one plus or minus the square root of two.
## The discriminant
The part under the square root, b squared minus four a c, is called the discriminant, because it discriminates between the cases.

If it is positive, there are two different solutions. If it is nought, the plus or minus adds and takes away nothing, so there is just one solution, sometimes called a repeated root. If it is negative, there is no ordinary square root, and so no ordinary solution.
?? How many solutions does x squared plus two x plus five equals nought have?
=> b squared minus four a c is four minus twenty, minus sixteen. Negative, so no ordinary solutions.
## The negative case, a door ajar

Mathematicians of the sixteenth century, solving harder equations in Italy, found themselves needing square roots of negative numbers even on the way to real answers. Gerolamo Cardano, in 1545, reluctantly wrote such a thing down and called it as subtle as it is useless. Rafael Bombelli, in 1572, worked out rules for calculating with them. Descartes called them imaginary, rather unkindly, and the name stuck. In my own century, Gauss and our own Hamilton made them entirely respectable, as complex numbers. With them, every quadratic has solutions. But that is a door I shall leave ajar for another evening.
## Summary

Completing the square turns x squared plus b x into, x plus half b, all squared, minus half b squared. Done once and for all, it gives the quadratic formula: x equals minus b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus four a c, over two a. The discriminant b squared minus four a c tells you whether there are two, one or no ordinary solutions. Next, parabolas: what quadratics look like. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. A sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule: two, four, six, eight. Mathematicians love them, because a good rule lets you jump straight to the hundredth or millionth term without walking through all the others. Tonight two great families of sequences, and a famous story, which may well be a legend.
## Terms and rules
Each number in a sequence is a term. The first term, the second term, and so on. We often call the general one, the nth term, where n stands for its position.
## Arithmetic sequences
Three, seven, eleven, fifteen. Each time we add four. A sequence that adds the same amount each time is called arithmetic, and the amount, here four, is the common difference.
To find the tenth term, do not count. Start at three, and to get from the first term to the tenth you add four nine times, not ten. Three plus thirty-six, thirty-nine.

In plain words: the nth term is the first term a, plus n minus one lots of the difference d. Why n minus one? Because the first term has had no differences added. It is the fencepost problem: ten posts in a straight fence have only nine gaps between them.
?? While I pour. What is the hundredth term of five, eight, eleven, fourteen and so on?
=> First term five, difference three. Five plus ninety-nine threes, five plus two hundred and ninety-seven, three hundred and two.
An arithmetic sequence is a straight line in disguise: plot term against position, and the points lie on a line with gradient d.
## Young Gauss and the sum

Now the story. Carl Friedrich Gauss, later the greatest mathematician of his age, was, so the tale goes, a small boy in a school in Brunswick, when the schoolmaster set the class to add all the numbers from one to a hundred, hoping for a quiet hour. Young Gauss wrote down the answer almost at once. The story was told by Gauss's friend Wolfgang Sartorius after his death, and it has grown in the retelling; the actual numbers may have been different. So, a legend with a kernel of truth, perhaps.

His trick: write the sum forwards and backwards. One plus a hundred is a hundred and one. Two plus ninety-nine, a hundred and one. Every pair makes a hundred and one, and there are fifty pairs. Fifty times a hundred and one is five thousand and fifty.
In plain words: the sum of the first n whole numbers is n times n plus one, over two.
?? What is the sum of the numbers from one to ten?
=> Ten times eleven over two, fifty-five.
## Geometric sequences

Now a different family. Two, six, eighteen, fifty-four. Each time we multiply by three. A sequence that multiplies by the same number each time is called geometric, and the multiplier is the common ratio.
The nth term is the first term times the ratio to the power of n minus one.

Geometric sequences grow alarmingly fast. There is an old legend, with versions from India and Persia, of the inventor of chess who asked his king for one grain of wheat on the first square of the board, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time. The sixty-fourth square alone would need two to the power of sixty-three grains, about nine million million million. More wheat than the world has ever grown.
?? Starting with one grain and doubling, how many grains are on the eleventh square?
=> Two to the power of ten, one thousand and twenty-four.
## Shrinking sequences

If the ratio is less than one, the terms shrink. One, a half, a quarter, an eighth. Add them up and something remarkable happens: the total gets closer and closer to two, but never passes it. Walk half the way to the door, then half the remaining way, and so on: you approach the door ever more closely. Adding infinitely many terms and getting a finite answer is the subject of a lecture at the summit, on series. Zeno of Elea built his famous paradoxes on exactly this puzzle, around four hundred and fifty years before Christ.
## Other famous sequences

The square numbers: one, four, nine, sixteen. The triangular numbers, made by stacking cannonballs in a triangle: one, three, six, ten, which are Gauss's sums. And the Fibonacci sequence, from Leonardo of Pisa's book of 1202, where each term is the sum of the two before: one, one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen. Fibonacci illustrated it with a rather unrealistic problem about breeding rabbits.
## Summary

An arithmetic sequence adds a common difference: the nth term is a plus, n minus one, times d. Gauss's trick sums one to n as n times n plus one over two. A geometric sequence multiplies by a common ratio and grows or shrinks fast. Shrinking geometric sums can approach a finite total, a taste of the summit. Next, algebraic fractions. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. You have met fractions at base camp: halves, quarters, and the art of adding them. Tonight the same fractions return, but with letters in them. I promise you there is nothing new to learn, only old rules in new clothes, and one famous blunder to avoid.
## The same rules
An algebraic fraction is simply a fraction with letters in it.

Three over x. Every rule you know for numerical fractions still holds, because the letters stand for numbers. With one condition: the bottom must never be nought. So in three over x, x must not be nought.
## Simplifying by cancelling
Six over eight simplifies to three over four, because six and eight share a factor of two. In the same way:
Top and bottom share three x. Six x divided by three x is two; nine x squared divided by three x is three x.
?? While I pour. Simplify ten a squared over five a.
=> Divide top and bottom by five a: two a.
## The famous blunder
Here it is. What is x plus three, over x?
⟦\frac{x+3}{x}⟧

It is tempting to cross out the x's, leaving three. That is wrong. Try x equals one: one plus three over one is four, not three. You may cancel factors, things multiplied, but never terms, things added. The x on top is not a factor of the whole top; it is only part of a sum, wrapped in the brown-paper parcel of the fraction line along with the three. You cannot take one item out of a sealed parcel.
The cure is always to factorise first, so that the parcels show.
Now x minus three is a factor of the top, a whole parcel, and it cancels with the bottom. Lovely.
?? Simplify x squared plus five x, over x.
=> Factorise the top: x times, bracket x plus five. Cancel the x. Answer: x plus five.
## Multiplying and dividing
Multiplying fractions: tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms.
⟦\frac{2}{x}\times\frac{x^{2}}{4}=\frac{2x^{2}}{4x}=\frac{x}{2}⟧
Dividing: flip the second fraction and multiply, exactly as at base camp.
⟦\frac{a}{3}\div\frac{a}{6}=\frac{a}{3}\times\frac{6}{a}=2⟧
## Adding and subtracting
To add a half and a third, we found a common denominator, six: three sixths plus two sixths, five sixths. With letters:
⟦\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}=\frac{y+x}{xy}⟧
The common denominator is x y. One over x becomes y over x y; one over y becomes x over x y. Add the tops.
?? Add one over x and two over x.
=> Same denominator already: three over x.
A slightly harder example:
The common denominator is x times, bracket x plus one. The first fraction becomes x plus one over that; the second becomes x over that. Tops add to two x plus one.
## Equations with fractions
To solve an equation full of fractions, multiply every term by the common denominator, and the fractions vanish, like Euclid the cat when the bath is drawn.
Multiply everything by six: three x plus two x equals sixty. Five x equals sixty; x is twelve. Check: six plus four is ten. Splendid.
## A useful old problem

One pipe fills a cistern in two hours; another fills it in three. Together? In an hour, the first fills a half, the second a third, together five sixths. So the whole takes six fifths of an hour: one hour and twelve minutes. Problems of this kind appear in Chinese, Indian and European arithmetic books for centuries. Mrs Blewitt applies the same reasoning to two maids polishing silver.
## Summary

Algebraic fractions follow the rules of ordinary fractions, with the bottom never nought. Cancel common factors, never terms: factorise first. Multiply tops and bottoms; divide by flipping; add with a common denominator. Clear fractions from equations by multiplying through. Next, a change of air: chance and probability. ## Letters and the balance

A letter stands for a number we do not yet know, or for any number at all. An equation is a balance scale: whatever you do to one side, do to the other. The word algebra comes from al-jabr, restoring, in the title of al-Khwarizmi's book of about 820. The equals sign is Robert Recorde's, from 1557: two parallel lines, because no two things are more equal.
## Expressions and like terms
Terms join into expressions. Like terms share exactly the same letters and powers, and combine.
x and x squared are not like terms. When multiplying terms, multiply numbers and gather letters: three x times four y is twelve x y.
## Substitution
Replace letters with numbers, follow BIDMAS, and bracket negative numbers.
If x is three: nine, times two, eighteen, plus one, nineteen. If x is minus three: bracket minus three squared is nine, so again nineteen.
?? If a is two and b is minus one, what is three a minus b?
=> Six minus, bracket, minus one: six plus one, seven.
## Solving
Undo operations in reverse order, coat before waistcoat. Gather letters on one side first.
Take three x: two x plus two equals ten. Take two: two x equals eight. Divide: x equals four. Check by substitution.
?? Solve x over three, plus two, equals six.
=> Take two: x over three equals four. Multiply by three: x equals twelve.
## Indices
Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices; dividing subtracts; a power of a power multiplies.
Anything to the power of nought is one. A negative power means one over. A power of a half is a square root.
## Rearranging
Changing the subject is solving with letters left as letters.
That is Fahrenheit to Celsius, obtained from F equals nine fifths C plus thirty-two by taking thirty-two from both sides and multiplying by five ninths.
?? Make r the subject of A equals pi r squared.
=> Divide by pi, then square root: r equals the square root of A over pi.
## Summary
Letters, balance, like terms, careful substitution, reverse-order solving, three laws of indices, and rearranging. That is the first stretch of the foothills. Onward, my dear friend.

A quadratic has x squared as its highest power.

They arise from areas and from motion. The Babylonians solved them four thousand years ago, and al-Khwarizmi in Baghdad, around 820, solved them by completing a square of tiles. A quadratic may have two solutions, one, or none among ordinary numbers.

If a product is nought, one factor is nought. Get nought on one side, and look for two numbers that multiply to the last number and add to the middle coefficient.

So x squared minus five x plus six equals nought gives x is two or three. With no plain number, take out x: x squared minus seven x is x times, bracket x minus seven, giving nought or seven. And never divide by x, or you lose nought.
?? While I pour. Solve x squared plus x minus six equals nought.
=> Numbers multiplying to minus six and adding to one: three and minus two. Bracket x plus three, bracket x minus two. So x is minus three or two.

Halve the middle coefficient, square the bracket, take away the corner.
So x squared plus ten x equals thirty-nine becomes bracket x plus five, squared, equals sixty-four, and x is three or minus thirteen.

$$ x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}

Minus b, plus or minus the square root of b squared minus four a c, all over two a. The discriminant, b squared minus four a c, decides the number of solutions: positive two, nought one, negative none.
?? How many solutions has x squared minus six x plus nine equals nought?
=> b squared minus four a c is thirty-six minus thirty-six, nought. Just one: x equals three.

Tonight, the foothills from the air: what algebra is, where it came from, and where it leads.
## What it is

Algebra is the part of mathematics that uses letters and other symbols for numbers, and studies how such symbols can be manipulated. At its simplest, it is arithmetic with unknowns: if three x plus two equals eleven, what is x? It lets us state rules for all numbers at once, such as the distributive law, and solve problems without knowing the answer in advance.
## The word

Around 820, in Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi wrote The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing. The Arabic word al-jabr, completion or restoring, meant moving a subtracted quantity to the other side of an equation, so that all the terms are positive. Al-muqabala, balancing, meant cancelling equal terms on both sides. In Latin translation, al-jabr became algebra. In medieval Spain, an algebrista was also a bone-setter, a restorer of broken bones; the word still means that in Spanish.
?? While I pour. In three x minus four equals eight, what does restoring do?
=> It moves the minus four across, adding four to both sides: three x equals twelve.
## Words before symbols

For most of its history, algebra was written in words. Al-Khwarizmi wrote a square and ten roots equal thirty-nine dirhams, which we would write x squared plus ten x equals thirty-nine. Symbols came slowly. Diophantus used some abbreviations. In 1557 Robert Recorde introduced the equals sign. In 1591 François Viète used letters for both unknowns and known quantities. And in 1637 Descartes gave us our habit of x, y and z for unknowns and a, b and c for known numbers, and the small raised numbers for powers.
## Elementary and abstract

Elementary algebra, the kind taught in schools, deals with expressions, equations and formulas in ordinary numbers. Linear and quadratic equations, simultaneous equations, factorising and expanding: the foothills we have climbed.

In my own century, algebra grew wings. Galois and Abel studied which equations can be solved by formulas, and found that the answer lay in the symmetries of their solutions. Hamilton found quaternions, where order of multiplication matters, and Cayley matrices. Boole made an algebra of logic. Mathematicians came to see that one can study any collection of objects with operations obeying rules, whether or not the objects are numbers. This is abstract algebra, with its groups, rings and fields. Emmy Noether, in the twentieth century, did more than anyone to give it its modern form.
## Why it matters

Algebra is the language in which most of mathematics, science and engineering is written. A formula in physics, a spreadsheet of accounts, the code of a computer: all are algebra. And the habit of mind it teaches, naming an unknown and reasoning about it, is useful far beyond mathematics.
## Summary

Algebra represents numbers by symbols and studies how to manipulate them. Its name comes from al-Khwarizmi's al-jabr, restoring, around 820. Symbols arrived slowly, through Recorde, Viète and Descartes. Abstract algebra, from the nineteenth century, studies structures such as groups, rings and fields.

## Variables

Elementary algebra is arithmetic with letters. A letter, such as x, stands for a number we do not know yet, or for any number at all. Such a letter is called a variable. In the equation x plus three equals seven, x is an unknown, to be found. In the statement a plus b equals b plus a, a and b are general: the rule is true whatever numbers they stand for.
## Expressions and equations

An expression is a combination of numbers, letters and operations, such as two x plus five. An equation says two expressions are equal, such as two x plus five equals thirteen. Expressions can be simplified, for example by collecting like terms: three x plus two x is five x. Brackets can be expanded: two times, x plus three, is two x plus six. Or factorised, in reverse.
?? While I pour. Simplify four x plus seven plus x minus two.
=> Five x plus five.
## Solving equations

An equation is like a pair of scales in balance. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, and the balance is kept. To solve two x plus five equals thirteen, take five from both sides, two x equals eight, then divide both sides by two: x equals four. Then check, by putting four back in: two fours and five is thirteen. Correct.
## Quadratics

A quadratic equation has an x squared in it. Some can be solved by factorising: x squared minus five x plus six equals nought factorises into, x minus two, times, x minus three, so x is two or three. For the rest there is the quadratic formula, which we met in the foothills.

## Simultaneous equations
Two unknowns need two clues. If x plus y equals ten, and x minus y equals two, add the equations: two x equals twelve, so x is six, and y is four.
?? Check: is six plus four ten, and six minus four two?
=> Yes on both counts.
## Inequalities and functions

Elementary algebra also handles inequalities, such as x plus two is greater than five, solved like equations, but with one trap: multiplying or dividing by a negative number turns the inequality round. And it introduces functions, rules that turn one number into another, which lead us up to the ridge.
## Summary

Elementary algebra uses variables for unknown or general numbers. It simplifies expressions, solves equations by doing the same to both sides, solves quadratics by factorising or by formula, and solves simultaneous equations by combining them. It is the gateway to functions and everything above.

In mathematics, a variable (from Latin variabilis 'changeable') is a symbol, typically a letter, that refers to an unspecified mathematical object. One says colloquially that the variable represents or denotes the object, and that any valid candidate for the object is the value of the variable. The values a variable can take are usually of the same kind, often numbers. More specifically, the values involved may form a set, such as the set of real numbers.

The object may not always exist, or it might be uncertain whether any valid candidate exists or not. For example, one could represent two integers by the variables ⟦p⟧ and ⟦q⟧ and require that the value of the square of ⟦p⟧ is twice the square of ⟦q⟧, which in algebraic notation can be written ⟦p^{2} = 2 q^{2}⟧. A definitive proof that this relationship is impossible to satisfy when ⟦p⟧ and ⟦q⟧ are restricted to nonzero integers isn't obvious, but it has been known since ancient times and has had a big influence on mathematics ever since.

Originally, the term variable was used primarily for the argument of a function, in which case its value could be thought of as varying within the domain of the function. This is the motivation for the choice of the term. Also, variables are used for denoting values of functions, such as the symbol ⟦y⟧ in the equation ⟦y = f(x)⟧, where ⟦x⟧ is the argument and ⟦f⟧ denotes the function itself.

A variable may represent an unspecified number that remains fixed during the resolution of a problem; in which case, it is often called a parameter. A variable may denote an unknown number that has to be determined; in which case, it is called an unknown; for example, in the quadratic equation ⟦ax^{2} + bx + c = 0⟧, the variables ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧, ⟦c⟧ are parameters, and ⟦x⟧ is the unknown.

Sometimes the same symbol can be used to denote both a variable and a constant, that is a well defined mathematical object. For example, the Greek letter ⟦π⟧ generally represents the number ⟦π⟧, but has also been used to denote a projection. Similarly, the letter ⟦e⟧ often denotes Euler's number, but has been used to denote an unassigned coefficient for quartic function and higher degree polynomials. Even the symbol ⟦1⟧ has been used to denote an identity element of an arbitrary field. These two notions are used almost identically, therefore one usually must be told whether a given symbol denotes a variable or a constant.
Variables are often used for representing matrices, functions, their arguments, sets and their elements, vectors, spaces, and so on
In mathematical logic, a variable is a symbol that either represents an unspecified constant of the theory, or is being quantified over.
## Early history

The earliest uses of an "unknown quantity" date back to at least the Ancient Egyptians with the Moscow Mathematical Papyrus (around 1500 BC) which described problems with unknowns rhetorically, called the "Aha problems". The "Aha problems" involve finding unknown quantities (referred to as aha, "stack") if the sum of the quantity and part(s) of it are given (The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus also contains four of these types of problems). For example, problem 19 asks one to calculate a quantity taken 1+1⁄2 times and added to 4 to make 10. In modern mathematical notation: a long formula. Around the same time in Mesopotamia, mathematics of the Old Babylonian period (around 2000 BC – 1500 BC) was more advanced, also studying quadratic and cubic equations.
In works of ancient Greece such as Euclid's Elements (around 300 BC), mathematics was described geometrically. For example, The Elements, proposition 1 of Book II, Euclid includes the proposition:

"If there be two straight lines, and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines is equal to the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments."

This corresponds to the algebraic identity ⟦a(b + c) = ab + ac⟧ (distributivity), but is described entirely geometrically. Euclid, and other greek geometers, also used single letters refer to geometric points and shapes. This kind of algebra is now sometimes called Greek geometric algebra.

Diophantus of Alexandria, pioneered a form of syncopated algebra in his Arithmetica (around 200 AD), which introduced symbolic manipulation of expressions with unknowns and powers, but without modern symbols for relations (such as equality or inequality) or exponents. An unknown number was called ⟦ζ⟧. The square of ⟦ζ⟧ was ⟦Δ^{v}⟧; the cube was ⟦K^{v}⟧; the fourth power was ⟦Δ^{v} Δ⟧; and the fifth power was ⟦Δ K^{v}⟧. ## Early modern period

At the end of the 16th century, François Viète introduced the idea of representing known and unknown numbers by letters, nowadays called variables, and the idea of computing with them as if they were numbers—in order to obtain the result by a simple replacement. Viète's convention was to use consonants for known values, and vowels for unknowns.

In 1637, René Descartes "invented the convention of representing unknowns in equations by ⟦x⟧, ⟦y⟧, and ⟦z⟧, and knowns by ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧, and ⟦c⟧". Contrarily to Viète's convention, Descartes' is still commonly in use. The history of the letter x in math was discussed in an 1887 Scientific American article.

Starting in the 1660s, Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz independently developed the infinitesimal calculus, which essentially consists of studying how an infinitesimal variation of a time-varying quantity, called a Fluent, induces a corresponding variation of another quantity which is a function of the first variable. Almost a century later, Leonhard Euler fixed the terminology of infinitesimal calculus, and introduced the notation ⟦y = f(x)⟧ for a function ⟦f⟧, its variable ⟦x⟧ and its value ⟦y⟧. ## Notation

Variables are generally denoted by a single letter, most often from the Latin alphabet and less often from the Greek, which may be lowercase or capitalized. The letter may be followed by a subscript: a number (as in ⟦x_{2}⟧), another variable (⟦xi⟧), a word or abbreviation of a word as a label (⟦x_{total}⟧) or a mathematical expression (⟦x_{2}i_{+1}⟧). Under the influence of computer science, some variable names in pure mathematics consist of several letters and digits. Following René Descartes (1596–1650), letters at the beginning of the alphabet such as ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧, ⟦c⟧ are commonly used for known values and parameters, and letters at the end of the alphabet such as ⟦x⟧, ⟦y⟧, ⟦z⟧ are commonly used for unknowns and variables of functions. In printed mathematics, the norm is to set variables and constants in an italic typeface.

For example, a general quadratic function is conventionally written as ⟦ax^{2} + bx + c⟧, where ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧ and ⟦c⟧ are parameters (also called constants, because they are constant functions), while ⟦x⟧ is the variable of the function. A more explicit way to denote this function is ⟦x ↦ ax^{2} + bx + c⟧, which clarifies the function-argument status of ⟦x⟧ and the constant status of ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧ and ⟦c⟧. Since ⟦c⟧ occurs in a term that is a constant function of ⟦x⟧, it is called the constant term.

Specific branches and applications of mathematics have specific naming conventions for variables. Variables with similar roles or meanings are often assigned consecutive letters or the same letter with different subscripts. For example, the three axes in 3D coordinate space are conventionally called ⟦x⟧, ⟦y⟧, and ⟦z⟧. In physics, the names of variables are largely determined by the physical quantity they describe, but various naming conventions exist. A convention often followed in probability and statistics is to use ⟦X⟧, ⟦Y⟧, ⟦Z⟧ for the names of random variables, keeping ⟦x⟧, ⟦y⟧, ⟦z⟧ for variables representing corresponding better-defined values.

## Specific kinds of variables
It is common for variables to play different roles in the same mathematical formula, and names or qualifiers have been introduced to distinguish them. For example, the general cubic equation

To distinguish them, the variable ⟦x⟧ is called an unknown, and the other variables are called parameters or coefficients, or sometimes constants, although this last terminology is incorrect for an equation, and should be reserved for the function defined by the left-hand side of this equation.

In the context of functions, the term variable refers commonly to the arguments of the functions. This is typically the case in sentences like "function of a real variable", "⟦x⟧ is the variable of the function ⟦f : x ↦ f(x)⟧", "⟦f⟧ is a function of the variable ⟦x⟧" (meaning that the argument of the function is referred to by the variable ⟦x⟧).

In the same context, variables that are independent of ⟦x⟧ define constant functions and are therefore called constant. For example, a constant of integration is an arbitrary constant function that is added to a particular antiderivative to obtain the other antiderivatives. Because of the strong relationship between polynomials and polynomial functions, the term "constant" is often used to denote the coefficients of a polynomial, which are constant functions of the indeterminates.

An unknown is a variable in an equation which has to be solved for.

Formally speaking, an indeterminate is not a variable, but a constant in the polynomial ring or the ring of formal power series. However, because of the strong relationship between polynomials or power series and the functions that they define, many authors consider indeterminates as a special kind of variables.

A parameter is a quantity (usually a number) which is a part of the input of a problem, and remains constant during the whole solution of this problem. For example, in mechanics the mass and the size of a solid body are parameters for the study of its movement. In computer science, parameter has a different meaning and denotes an argument of a function.

## Dependent and independent variables

In calculus and its application to physics and other sciences, it is rather common to consider a variable, say ⟦y⟧, whose possible values depend on the value of another variable, say ⟦x⟧. In mathematical terms, the dependent variable ⟦y⟧ represents the value of a function of ⟦x⟧. To simplify formulas, it is often useful to use the same symbol for the dependent variable ⟦y⟧ and the function mapping ⟦x⟧ onto ⟦y⟧. For example, the state of a physical system depends on measurable quantities such as the pressure, the temperature, the spatial position,..., and all these quantities vary when the system evolves, that is, they are function of the time. In the formulas describing the system, these quantities are represented by variables which are dependent on the time, and thus considered implicitly as functions of the time.
Therefore, in a formula, a dependent variable is a variable that is implicitly a function of another (or several other) variables. An independent variable is a variable that is not dependent.

The property of a variable to be dependent or independent depends often of the point of view and is not intrinsic. For example, in the notation ⟦f(x, y, z)⟧, the three variables may be all independent and the notation represents a function of three variables. On the other hand, if ⟦y⟧ and ⟦z⟧ depend on ⟦x⟧ (are dependent variables) then the notation represents a function of the single independent variable ⟦x⟧.

## Moduli spaces
Considering constants and variables can lead to the concept of moduli spaces. For illustration, consider the equation for a parabola,
$$ y = a x^{2} + b x + c

where ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧, ⟦c⟧, ⟦x⟧ and ⟦y⟧ are all considered to be real. The set of points ⟦(x, y)⟧ in the 2D plane satisfying this equation trace out the graph of a parabola. Here, ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧ and ⟦c⟧ are regarded as constants, which specify the parabola, while ⟦x⟧ and ⟦y⟧ are variables.

Then instead regarding ⟦a⟧, ⟦b⟧ and ⟦c⟧ as variables, we observe that each set of 3-tuples ⟦(a, b, c)⟧ corresponds to a different parabola. That is, they specify coordinates on the 'space of parabolas': this is known as a moduli space of parabolas.

In mathematics, an equation is a mathematical formula that expresses the equality of two expressions, by connecting them with the equals sign =. The word equation and its cognates in other languages may have subtly different meanings; for example, in French an équation is defined as containing one or more variables while an égalité does not require variables, but in English, any well-formed formula consisting of two expressions related with an equals sign is an equation.

Solving an equation containing variables consists of determining which values of the variables make the equality true. The variables for which the equation has to be solved are also called unknowns, and the values of the unknowns that satisfy the equality are called solutions of the equation. There are two kinds of equations: identities and conditional equations. An identity is true for all values of the variables. A conditional equation is only true for particular values of the variables.
The "=" symbol, which appears in every equation, was invented in 1557 by Robert Recorde, who considered that nothing could be more equal than parallel straight lines with the same length.
## Description

An equation is written as two expressions, connected by an equals sign ("="). The expressions on the two sides of the equals sign are called the "left-hand side" and "right-hand side" of the equation. Very often the right-hand side of an equation is assumed to be zero. This does not reduce the generality, as this can be realized by subtracting the right-hand side from both sides.
The most common type of equation is a polynomial equation (commonly called also an algebraic equation) in which the two sides are polynomials.
